subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What is primary data in a geographical fieldwork enquiry?
options: Data collected first-hand by the investigator during fieldwork
Data taken from a published government census
Data copied from a textbook or website
Data that is always presented as opinions
questions.explain: Primary data is original data that the student collects themselves in the field, such as their own measurements or survey results.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of secondary data?
options: Population figures obtained from a national census
River depth you measured with a metre rule
A questionnaire you handed out to shoppers
A pedestrian count you carried out yourself
questions.explain: Secondary data is information collected by someone else, such as census figures, maps or published statistics.

questions.q: In fieldwork, what is a hypothesis?
options: A testable statement that the investigation aims to prove or disprove
A final conclusion written before collecting data
A method used to present data as a graph
A list of hazards identified on a risk assessment
questions.explain: A hypothesis is a predictive, testable statement whose validity is judged against the evidence collected.

questions.q: What does quantitative data consist of?
options: Numerical data that can be counted or measured
Descriptive data based on opinions and feelings
Photographs and field sketches only
Data that cannot be shown on a graph
questions.explain: Quantitative data is numerical, for example traffic counts or river velocity readings, and can be analysed statistically.

questions.q: Which of these best describes qualitative data?
options: Descriptive information such as opinions, views and field sketches
Measurements of river width in metres
The number of vehicles passing in ten minutes
Percentages calculated from a survey
questions.explain: Qualitative data is descriptive and non-numerical, capturing opinions, impressions and observations.

questions.q: What is systematic sampling?
options: Collecting data at regular, fixed intervals
Collecting data at randomly chosen points
Collecting data only where it is easy to reach
Collecting data in proportion to subgroups in a population
questions.explain: Systematic sampling takes readings at set intervals, for example every 10 metres or every fifth person.

questions.q: How is the mean of a data set calculated?
options: Add all the values together and divide by the number of values
Choose the value that occurs most often
Find the middle value when data are placed in order
Subtract the smallest value from the largest value
questions.explain: The mean is the arithmetic average: the sum of all values divided by how many values there are.

questions.q: What is the median of a set of data?
options: The middle value when the data are arranged in order
The most frequently occurring value
The average of all the values
The difference between the highest and lowest values
questions.explain: The median is the central value once the data are ranked from smallest to largest.

questions.q: Why is a risk assessment carried out before fieldwork?
options: To identify potential hazards and plan how to reduce risks to safety
To decide which graphs to draw afterwards
To calculate the mean and median of results
To choose a hypothesis to investigate
questions.explain: A risk assessment anticipates hazards, such as fast-flowing water or traffic, and sets out ways to minimise them.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly represents the stages of a geographical enquiry?
options: Ask a question, collect data, present data, analyse, conclude, evaluate
Collect data, ask a question, conclude, present data, evaluate
Conclude, evaluate, collect data, present data, analyse
Present data, collect data, ask a question, evaluate, conclude
questions.explain: The enquiry moves logically from posing a question through collecting and presenting data to analysis, conclusion and evaluation.

questions.q: Which of these is the most suitable question for a manageable GCSE fieldwork enquiry?
options: How does environmental quality change with distance from the town centre?
Why do all cities in the world grow?
Is climate change real everywhere on Earth?
What causes every river in the country to flood?
questions.explain: A good enquiry question is focused, local and answerable with the primary data a student can realistically collect.

questions.q: What is an advantage of using random sampling in fieldwork?
options: It reduces bias because every point has an equal chance of being chosen
It guarantees data are collected at exactly even intervals
It ensures the easiest sites are always selected
It removes the need to collect any secondary data
questions.explain: Random sampling avoids deliberately favouring particular sites, so it reduces bias in the data collected.

questions.q: What does a choropleth map show?
options: Differences in a value between areas using shading of increasing density
The flow of movement between two places using arrows
Individual data points plotted against two variables
A cross-section of the land along a line
questions.explain: A choropleth map uses graded shading, with darker shades showing higher values, to compare areas.

questions.q: Which presentation technique best shows the proportion of different land uses in a town centre?
options: A pie chart
A line graph
A scatter graph
A cross-section
questions.explain: A pie chart displays how a whole is divided into parts, making proportions of land use easy to compare.

questions.q: What does the range of a data set tell you?
options: The spread between the highest and lowest values
The most common value in the data
The middle value of the data
The average of all the values
questions.explain: The range is found by subtracting the smallest value from the largest and shows how spread out the data are.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of evaluating a fieldwork enquiry?
options: To judge the reliability of the data and suggest improvements
To collect additional primary data in the field
To draw the first graphs of the results
To write the original hypothesis
questions.explain: Evaluation reflects on limitations, accuracy and reliability of methods and data, and proposes how the enquiry could be improved.

questions.q: A student wants to survey pedestrians so that the number questioned in each age group matches the proportion of that age group in the town's population. Which sampling method should they use?
options: Stratified sampling
Random sampling
Systematic sampling
Opportunistic sampling
questions.explain: Stratified sampling divides the population into subgroups and samples each in proportion to its size.

questions.q: Using the float method, an orange takes 20 seconds to travel 10 metres down a river. What is the river's surface velocity?
options: 2 m/s
questions.explain: Velocity equals distance divided by time, so 10 m ÷ 20 s = 0.5 m/s.

questions.q: A student records these pedestrian counts: 2, 4, 6, 8, 9. What is the median value?
questions.explain: With five ordered values, the median is the third (middle) value, which is 6.

questions.q: A student wants to judge how attractive and well-maintained different streets appear. Which method is most appropriate?
options: An environmental quality survey using bipolar scoring
A river velocity measurement
A national census download
A discharge calculation
questions.explain: An environmental quality survey uses bipolar scales to rate features such as litter and building condition, judging the quality of a place.
